prompt.context: GSK has a prescription migraine medicine, IMITREX, which belongs to a class of medicines called triptans. IMITREX was the first medicine in this class (introduced to the US market in 1993) and has patent protection in the US until 2009. It remains the market leader despite the emergence of 5 direct competitors in the triptan class. Triptans compete with other nonspecific prescription pain relievers. IMITREX also competes with over-the-counter (OTC) headache products. The volume of OTC use is at least 10-fold higher than prescription medicines for migraine. An IMITREX prescription for 10 tablets costs approximately $150 at the retail pharmacy level (1 tablet per migraine headache), although many patients have health insurance and pay a co-pay of $20–$30 per prescription. OTC headache medicines cost approximately $5 for a bottle of 30 tablets (2 tablets per headache).
prompt.question: GSK is considering switching IMITREX from prescription (Rx) to over-the-counter (OTC). How would you structure your analysis and determine if this was the right direction for the brand? If you were going to switch from Rx to OTC, when do you think it should occur in the lifecycle of the product? Would you need any additional information? Would any competitive issues change your decision or affect your analysis?

clarifying_info.q: Are there any new entrants expected in the prescription migraine market?
What type of conversion rate is expected in the OTC market?
Do we have any information on the price elasticity of demand in the migraine market?

framework: Understand the current Rx business: revenue, margins, patient base, and competitive position among triptans
Assess the OTC opportunity: market size (OTC use is ~10x Rx), addressable customer expansion, and willingness to pay at OTC price points
Pricing analysis: determine the OTC price per pill consumers would accept (~$2–$3/pill) and back into required volume to maintain current revenue
Timing: evaluate when in the patent lifecycle to switch — ideally just before patent expiration to pre-empt generics and lock in brand equity with OTC consumers
Competitive implications: impact of 5 existing triptan competitors and potential generic entrants post-2009; risk of cannibalization vs. incremental share
Regulatory and distribution considerations: FDA Rx-to-OTC switch process, channel changes, marketing investment required
Consumer behavior: risk of over-medication and inappropriate use if available OTC

questions.prompt: At what OTC price per pill would consumers likely be willing to purchase IMITREX, and what does that imply for a bottle price?
questions.guidance: Consumers are accustomed to paying $2–$3 per pill when purchasing OTC (co-pay of $20–$30 / 10 tablets = $2–$3/pill). Paying more than ~$3/pill is unlikely given OTC alternatives at much lower prices. A 10-tablet OTC bottle at $2–$3/pill implies a $20–$30 retail price.

math.setup: Current effective price per pill to insured patient: $20–$30 co-pay / 10 tablets. OTC consumer ceiling: $2–$3 per pill. Implied OTC bottle price (10 tablets): $2–$3 × 10 = $20–$30.
steps: OTC bottle (10 tablets) price ceiling = $2.00 × 10 to $3.00 × 10 = $20 to $30
math.answer: OTC price ceiling roughly $20–$30 for 10 tablets (~$2–$3 per pill).

questions.prompt: What minimum OTC volume (relative to current Rx volume) would GSK need to maintain current revenue, given the lower OTC price?
questions.guidance: Current Rx price is $150/10 tablets. If OTC price is $15/bottle (minimum feasible plus some margin), GSK would need a 10x volume increase to match revenue — which is plausible given OTC market is ~10x larger. More conservatively, at a $20–$30 OTC price, the required volume multiplier is lower.

math.setup: Revenue parity: Rx revenue = OTC revenue. Let Rx units = 1 (index). Rx revenue per unit = $150. OTC price per unit = $15 (minimum scenario). Required OTC units = $150 / $15 = 10. OTC market is ~10x Rx market — so volume uplift is feasible in theory.
steps: OTC market volume is stated as at least 10x Rx market — volume parity is plausible
At $20–$30 OTC price, required multiple = $150/$30 to $150/$20 = 5x to 7.5x — even more achievable
math.answer: GSK needs roughly a 5–10x volume increase at OTC prices of $20–$30 to match current Rx revenue; the OTC market is ~10x larger so the scale exists.

questions.prompt: When in the product lifecycle should the Rx-to-OTC switch occur?
questions.guidance: Conversion should happen close to patent expiration (2009) but before full expiration. Switching early enough allows GSK to build OTC brand loyalty and convert existing Rx patients before generic triptans flood the market. Switching too early sacrifices lucrative Rx revenue unnecessarily. The optimal window is approximately 1–2 years before patent expiry.

questions.prompt: What competitive and behavioral risks should GSK consider?
questions.guidance: Key risks: (1) Current insured Rx patients paying only $20–$30 co-pay face little incentive to switch to OTC; (2) Patients may over-medicate (use for ordinary headaches) driving misuse and potential safety issues; (3) Generic entry post-2009 will erode Rx revenue regardless — OTC move is partly defensive; (4) 5 existing triptan competitors may also pursue OTC, intensifying shelf competition; (5) OTC converts brand from prescribed medicine to consumer product, changing marketing dynamics significantly.

brainstorming.prompt: What factors should GSK evaluate when deciding whether and when to switch IMITREX from Rx to OTC?

categories.name: Financial / Revenue
ideas: Current Rx revenue and margin structure
OTC price point consumers will accept
Required volume uplift to break even
Impact on branded vs. generic revenue post-2009
Distribution cost differences (pharmacy vs. mass retail)

categories.name: Market Size & Demand
ideas: OTC migraine/headache market is ~10x prescription market in volume
Conversion rate of Rx patients to OTC unknown
Potential to capture OTC headache sufferers who never saw a doctor
Risk of cannibalizing existing insured Rx patients who pay only co-pay

categories.name: Timing & Patent Lifecycle
ideas: Patent expires 2009 — generics will enter unless OTC brand established
Switch just before expiry to pre-empt generic erosion
Early switch sacrifices high Rx margin unnecessarily
Brand equity built OTC is harder for generics to replicate

categories.name: Competitive
ideas: No new Rx entrants expected
5 existing triptan competitors — may also pursue OTC
Generic triptan competition post-2009
OTC competition from non-specific analgesics (Advil, Tylenol, Excedrin)

categories.name: Consumer Behavior
ideas: Insured patients pay low co-pay now — low incentive to seek OTC
Patients may over-medicate if OTC (use for regular headaches)
Some patients self-diagnose and prefer OTC convenience
Brand recognition may drive preference over generics

categories.name: Regulatory & Operational
ideas: FDA Rx-to-OTC switch requires new clinical/safety data
Labeling changes and self-selection guidance needed
Different distribution channels (retail, grocery, online)
Marketing shift from physician detailing to consumer advertising

recommendation: GSK should plan a phased Rx-to-OTC switch timed approximately 1–2 years before the 2009 patent expiration
At a $20–$30 OTC price point, a 5–10x volume uplift is plausible given the OTC migraine market is ~10x larger, making the switch financially viable
Establishing a strong OTC brand before generic entry is the key strategic rationale
risks: Consumer willingness to pay above OTC norms for a migraine-specific drug is uncertain
Insured Rx patients have little incentive to self-pay OTC; net new volume must come from non-Rx migraine sufferers
Over-medication and misuse risk if available without prescription
Competitors may execute a similar OTC switch, eroding first-mover advantage
next_steps: Commission consumer price sensitivity research to validate $2–$3/pill OTC willingness to pay
Estimate realistic Rx-to-OTC conversion rates with market research
Model revenue scenarios across OTC price points ($15, $20, $30 per 10 tablets) and volume multiples
Begin FDA Rx-to-OTC switch filing process early given multi-year timeline
Develop OTC brand and consumer marketing strategy
